Round~6 carried round~5's remedy to GGUF and tested two of our setup's choices, under a plan pushed to a hosted repository after plumbing checks and smoke runs on validation items and before any of its models was trained (results: Table~\ref{tab:round6} in Appendix~\ref{app:extra}). llama.cpp can apply a LoRA at load time on top of a quantized model, so a GGUF adapter can be trained against the weights its file ships: we dequantized every tensor of the Qwen3-0.6B base's Q3\_K\_M file, trained the gentle LoRA in bf16 on those values with the round-1 settings, converted it to a GGUF adapter and served it on the same file (Appendix~\ref{app:extra}). The converted adapter passed the plan's checks on validation items. All comparisons in the round use round-6 evaluations.

At Q3\_K\_M the gentle LoRA trained against the shipped weights delivered 0.986 [0.965, 1.009] of the bf16 gain, against $R = 0.795$ [0.771, 0.819] fused and quantized. The bf16-trained adapter applied at load time, its update stored in float32 and never quantized, delivered 0.733 [0.709, 0.757], less than the fused model (a paired difference of $-0.062$ [$-0.082$, $-0.042$], post hoc); training against the shipped weights beat it by $+0.253$ [$+0.229$, $+0.279$], the plan's pre-specified contrast. As the plan predicted, training against the shipped weights recovered more than half of the fused model's loss, exceeding halfway by $+0.089$ [$+0.071$, $+0.108$] (W6-H1 supported), and the load-time adapter recovered less, falling short by 0.164 [0.146, 0.183] (W6-H2 supported). At Q2\_K, where the base scores 0\%, training against the shipped weights helped both LoRAs; at Q3\_K\_M it cost the strong LoRA 0.115 of $R$, as at MLX~4-bit (exploratory; Appendix~\ref{app:extra}).

Trained with mlx-lm's other defaults (1,000 steps, LoRA on the last 16 of 28 layers, no prompt masking), a gentle and a strong Qwen3-0.6B LoRA both learned the task, gaining 66.6 and 73.1 points at MLX bf16, and unlike in our eight settings the LoRA at $10^{-4}$ was the more accurate one at bf16 (80.7\% against 74.2\%). It again kept more of its gain, by $+0.479$ [$+0.449$, $+0.509$] in $R$ at Q3\_K\_M and $+0.259$ [$+0.231$, $+0.286$] at MLX~4-bit (W6-H3 supported); at Q3\_K\_M the default gentle LoRA kept 0.38 of its gain, against 0.795 for ours. Where the base breaks, neither default LoRA held on: both kept at most 0.4\% of their gain at MLX~3-bit and none at Q2\_K, where our strong LoRA kept 0.868 (exploratory).

An importance matrix computed on WikiText-2 narrowed the gap on both models without closing it. At Q3\_K\_M it raised the gentle Qwen3-0.6B LoRA's $R$ from 0.795 to 0.889 and narrowed its gap to the strong LoRA from 0.215 to 0.146, by less than half. On OLMo-2 1B, whose LoRAs both kept their full gain at Q3\_K\_M ($R$ of 1.02 and 1.08), the gap fell from 0.059 to 0.034 because the strong LoRA's $R$ fell; whether by less than half was inconclusive there, and so was W6-H4, which needed both models.

At MLX~3-bit and GGUF~Q3\_K\_M, the gentle LoRA kept less of its gain than the strong one in 10 of 10 pre-registered tests across three base models and two tasks, and also at Q3\_K\_M and MLX~4-bit with mlx-lm's other defaults (F1); it kept a smaller share of its accuracy at all five formats compared, 40 of 40 (F2). The loss did not come from rounding the update: keeping it exact recovered 5\% and 12\% of the loss in MLX and, post hoc, did worse than fusing in GGUF (F4), while training the gentle LoRA against the weights that ship delivered 96\% of the bf16 gain at MLX~4-bit and 99\% at Q3\_K\_M, against 84\% and 79\% (F5). The weight measurements describe these losses but have not been shown to predict them better than the size of the update (F6). In practice, select a fine-tune on the quantized artifact it will ship as (F3), and if a gentle LoRA must ship at a format where it loses its gain, train it against those weights: on the quantized base in MLX, or on the dequantized file, served as an adapter, in llama.cpp. We tested this on Qwen3-0.6B with one task and one seed per LoRA, and the same step cost the strong LoRA 0.158 of $R$ at MLX~4-bit and 0.115 at Q3\_K\_M. An importance matrix narrowed the gap without closing it (F8).

Round~6 rebuilt each training model for an adapter trained against the shipped weights from the base GGUF file: gguf-py dequantized every tensor, including the shared embedding, and the values were rounded to bf16; all 310 tensors of the rebuilt model matched that dequantization before training. The LoRA was trained with the round-1 settings, rewritten in PEFT form (lora\_alpha 160, so that llama.cpp's $\alpha/r$ equals mlx-lm's scale of 20) and converted with llama.cpp's \texttt{convert\_lora\_to\_gguf.py} in float32; for all 196 adapted modules, the update read back from the file matched mlx-lm's to within $10^{-15}$, relative. llama-server applied the adapter at scale~1 on the file it was trained against. On the 499 validation items, the load-time adapter gave the same predictions as its fused model at bf16 and 99.0\% of them on an 8-bit base, and loaded at scale~0 it agreed with the base model on 99.4\%. Round-6 evaluations decoded MLX models in batches of 32 and ran llama-server with four slots and without its host-memory prompt cache, settings that can change predictions near ties, so round-6 numbers are compared only with each other. Every Qwen3-0.6B GGUF file in the round, base included, was built around one shared embedding, as the fused fine-tunes are (Appendix~\ref{app:repro}); OLMo-2 1B does not tie its embeddings.

In round~6's exploratory arms (Table~\ref{tab:round6}), at Q2\_K, where the base scores 0\%, the gentle LoRA kept none of its gain fused or at load time and 0.947 when trained against the shipped weights. Trained against the shipped weights, the strong LoRA did worse at Q3\_K\_M, where it already keeps its gain, 0.895 against 1.010 ($-0.115$ [$-0.137$, $-0.094$]), as at MLX~4-bit in round~5, and better at Q2\_K, 1.024 against 0.868 ($+0.156$ [$+0.131$, $+0.182$]), whereas at MLX~3-bit in round~5 it made no difference. With mlx-lm's defaults, both LoRAs kept at most 0.4\% of their gain at MLX~3-bit and none at Q2\_K; at Q4\_K\_M they kept 0.85 and 0.93, and the strong LoRA was the more accurate (78.2\% against 66.9\%), unlike in our eight settings. Their update norms were 14.3 and 66.6, a ratio of 4.7 against 8.7 to 12.9 in rounds 1 to 4; the default gentle update was larger than our gentle LoRA's (9.5, Table~\ref{tab:grid}) yet kept less of its gain at Q3\_K\_M (0.38 against 0.795). On OLMo-2 1B the importance matrix left the gentle LoRA's $R$ at Q3\_K\_M almost unchanged (1.019 and 1.020) and lowered the strong one's from 1.078 to 1.054. At Q2\_K the matrix lifted the gentle Qwen3-0.6B LoRA from 0 to 0.35 of its gain, against 1.00 for the strong one.

In all 10 pre-registered tests (five fine-tune pairs, each at MLX~3-bit and GGUF~Q3\_K\_M), a LoRA trained at learning rate $10^{-4}$ retained more of its gain than the same LoRA at $10^{-5}$, mlx-lm's default learning rate, by $+0.06$ to $+0.63$ in $R$; with mlx-lm's other defaults, the gap at Q3\_K\_M was $+0.48$, but at MLX~3-bit both LoRAs lost almost all of their gain.

In exploratory comparisons over eight settings and five formats, the $10^{-5}$ LoRA kept a smaller share of its own accuracy in 40 of 40 cases, yet remained the more accurate model at Q4\_K\_M in all eight settings, while the $10^{-4}$ LoRA was the more accurate one at MLX~3-bit and Q2\_K in all eight.

For Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, whose checkpoints store a separate copy of their tied output head, the base GGUF files quantized the input embedding at each file's base type, while every fused fine-tune shares one embedding that llama-quantize keeps at Q6\_K.
